strengths: The task is relevant to speech processing and accessible communication. Combining EMG features, self-supervised speech units, and pretrained synthesis components is a plausible approach to reducing task-specific training requirements.

The representation analysis spans multiple self-supervised models and layers, reports held-out correlations up to r = 0.85, and includes acoustic-spectrogram comparisons. The separate gesture experiment covers 12 participants and provides complementary evidence that EMG power contains articulatory information.

The feature comparisons provide useful empirical evidence: full covariance features improve unit error rate from 64.18% to 58.70% and phoneme error rate from 53.79% to 41.42% relative to the tested spectral features.

The reported nine-hour corpus, approximately 6,800-word vocabulary, natural speaking rate, and sentence-disjoint test set are promising resources. Electrode placement and basic signal preprocessing are described clearly.
weaknesses: The central speech-synthesis claim is insufficiently evaluated. Tables 1–2 measure discrete-unit and phoneme prediction, not synthesized speech intelligibility or quality. Section 6 explicitly defers perceptual assessment and WER/CER to future work. With a best UER of 58.70%, intelligible synthesis cannot be inferred without evaluating generated audio and an oracle-unit synthesis reference. This missing evidence is a decisive reason for recommending revision rather than Findings.

The speech-data protocol omits essential information: participant and session counts, whether articulation was voiced or silent, how target audio was obtained, and how audio and EMG were aligned for frame-level regression. The 12 participants belong to a separate gesture dataset. Sentence-disjoint splits alone do not establish generalization across speakers, sessions, or electrode placements.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper omits training hyperparameters, detailed architecture configuration, feature normalization, linear-probe fitting and correlation aggregation procedures, and the number of runs and meaning of the reported ± values. The exact synthesis checkpoint, waveform-generation procedure, and handling of repeated HuBERT units under CTC are unclear. Data/code release is promised upon project completion, despite the claim that the corpus is open-sourced.

The articulatory interpretation exceeds the evidence. Predicting EMG power from speech representations supports an association, but does not establish that the models encode articulatory mechanisms rather than correlated acoustic energy, speech activity, or phonetic content. The separate sustained-gesture experiment does not resolve this distinction. Controls for these factors and uncertainty estimates are needed; agreement with a previously preferred HuBERT layer is not a direct mechanistic explanation of downstream performance.

Comparative evidence is narrow. Only three input representations are tested within one adapted architecture, without an established EMG-to-speech baseline on the same split. The power-to-SSL argument also does not establish superiority for the inverse synthesis task. Claims concerning efficiency, robustness to distribution shifts, and few-shot or zero-shot potential remain untested, and comparisons with invasive BCI systems do not provide a controlled benchmark.

Several methodological statements need correction or qualification: 31 × 31 features yield 961 dimensions, not 991; uniform chance accuracy for 13 gestures is approximately 7.7%, not 10%; clustering accuracy requires a specified cluster-to-label matching procedure; and PER and UER are not directly comparable measures of decoding difficulty. The assertion that spectral or rectified EMG features cannot be probed for gesture structure overlooks straightforward temporal pooling.

strengths: The problem is relevant to speech processing and assistive communication. Using pretrained speech representations and a frozen synthesis component is a plausible way to reduce the training burden for EMG-to-speech systems.

The representation comparisons provide useful preliminary evidence: full covariance features achieve 58.7% unit error rate and 41.42% phoneme error rate, outperforming the spectral features under the reported TDS setup. The compact, 31-dimensional power representation also performs competitively.

The paper combines a separate 12-participant gesture experiment with linear probes across several speech-model families. The reported corpus has substantial vocabulary coverage, and excluding test sentences from training and validation is a positive design choice.
weaknesses: The central speech-synthesis claim is not adequately evaluated. Tables 1–2 measure discrete-unit and phoneme prediction, with substantial remaining errors; neither establishes intelligible synthesized speech. There is no listening evaluation, synthesized-speech WER, or perceptual-quality assessment. Section 6 explicitly leaves these evaluations to future work. A ground-truth-unit resynthesis baseline would also help separate decoder errors from synthesis limitations.

The speech-data protocol is materially underspecified. Section 3 does not report the number of speech participants, recording sessions, their allocation across splits, or whether articulation was voiced or silent. It also does not explain how the reference audio was obtained. The 12 participants in Section 5.1 belong to a separate gesture dataset. Consequently, the scope of generalization and relevance to silent or impaired speech cannot be established.

The linear-probing result supports predictability, but the mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Shared speech activity, amplitude envelopes, and phonetic content could contribute to the correlation. Isolated-gesture clustering does not establish that the predicted components encode specific articulatory mechanisms during continuous speech. Appropriate activity/envelope controls, per-channel results, and uncertainty estimates are needed. The coincidence between HuBERT layer 6 and a previously useful synthesis layer is not a direct explanation of downstream performance.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a clear Findings recommendation. Missing details include audio–EMG alignment for the framewise probes, feature normalization and regression fitting, exact model checkpoints, TDS configuration, optimization and model selection, the number of runs, and the meaning of the reported ± values. The synthesis backend and handling of unit repetitions and durations are also insufficiently specified. Code and data are promised only upon project completion, despite the stronger open-source framing in the introduction.

The experiments compare feature representations within one architecture but do not establish the merits of the proposed pipeline against existing EMG-to-speech systems or a direct acoustic-prediction baseline. The claim that stronger forward linear predictability makes a representation the most effective inverse mapping pathway requires downstream comparisons across speech representations and layers. Electrode-shift robustness, efficiency, and adaptation benefits remain motivations rather than demonstrated results.

Several analytical statements need correction or qualification. Chance accuracy for 13 balanced gesture classes is approximately 7.7%, not 10%; the cluster-to-label scoring procedure is unspecified. A 31×31 matrix has 961 entries, not the stated 991. Spectral and rectified features can be temporally pooled, so dismissing them as inherently unavailable for fixed-dimensional probing is unjustified. PER and UER use different target inventories and sequence lengths, making their numerical comparison insufficient to conclude that phonemes are decoded more accurately.

strengths: The paper addresses an important speech-technology problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech generation with limited training data and unknown temporal alignment. Its connection to self-supervised speech representations is relevant to NLP and assistive communication.

The representation analysis provides promising evidence: held-out linear prediction of EMG power reaches approximately r = 0.85, and the separate 12-participant gesture experiment demonstrates substantial articulatory discriminability.

The feature comparisons show consistent benefits from covariance information. Full covariance features reduce unit error rate from 64.18% to 58.70% and phoneme error rate from 53.79% to 41.42% relative to the tested spectrogram features.

The reported nine-hour corpus, approximately 6,800-word vocabulary, natural articulation rate, and sentence-disjoint test set are potentially valuable. Electrode placement and signal preprocessing are described clearly.
weaknesses: The central speech-synthesis claim is not adequately evaluated. Tables 1–2 measure discrete-unit and phoneme decoding, whereas Section 6 explicitly leaves synthesized-audio quality, WER, and CER to future work. Neither listener evaluation nor an objective intelligibility assessment establishes that the proposed pipeline produces usable speech. A 58.70% unit error rate cannot by itself establish synthesis quality. This missing endpoint evaluation is the principal reason for recommending revision rather than Findings.

Essential experimental details are missing. The main speech corpus lacks participant and session counts, their allocation across splits, and a clear account of whether articulation is voiced or silent. The source and recording procedure for target audio, and its temporal correspondence to EMG in the linear probe, are insufficiently specified. Sentence-disjoint evaluation alone does not establish generalization across people or recording sessions.

The articulatory interpretation exceeds the evidence. Predicting aggregate muscle power from speech features and separately clustering sustained gestures supports an association, but does not demonstrate that the speech representations encode specific articulatory mechanisms during connected speech. Controls for acoustic energy, speech/silence structure, and temporal autocorrelation are needed. The claimed mechanistic explanation for HuBERT layer 6 is especially strong without a downstream comparison across layers.

Reproduction is currently difficult: optimizer settings, training schedule, detailed architecture configuration, feature normalization, linear-probe fitting and correlation aggregation, run counts, and the meaning of the reported error bars are unspecified. The exact pretrained synthesis checkpoint and treatment of repeated units and duration in CTC decoding also need clarification. Data and code are promised only upon project completion, despite the stronger open-source language elsewhere.

The synthesis experiments compare three input representations within one architecture but do not establish competitiveness with existing EMG-to-speech methods or the benefit of self-supervised targets over conventional acoustic targets. The adopted TDS–CTC–unit-synthesis pipeline is largely assembled from existing components; its empirical contribution needs stronger comparative validation.

Some methodological assertions require correction or qualification. Temporal pooling would permit fixed-dimensional spectrogram or rectified-signal comparisons, contrary to Section 5.1's dismissal of such probes. The stated random baseline for 13 balanced gesture classes should be approximately 7.7%, not 10%, and the conversion of unsupervised clusters into classification accuracy is not explained.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important speech-generation problem: learning from EMG and transcripts without temporally aligned audio supervision. The demonstration with silently articulated speech from a participant with ALS is a meaningful proof of concept.

The controlled feature comparisons support the usefulness of covariance representations. On DATA_GENERAL, full covariance features reduce UER from 62.71% to 56.08% and PER from 44.40% to 32.78% relative to equally dimensional spectrogram features. Results averaged over five seeds and consistent improvements on DATA_ALS strengthen this evidence.
Phoneme-guided training yields additional, consistent unit-decoding improvements: UER decreases from 56.08% to 51.81% on DATA_GENERAL and from 52.29% to 46.98% on DATA_ALS.

Evaluation includes human transcriptions of all 460 test utterances, rather than relying exclusively on automatic recognition. The manuscript provides substantial architecture and optimization details, reports participant consent, and explicitly acknowledges limitations concerning longitudinal stability and participant coverage. The proposed datasets could be valuable community resources.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Predicting EMG power from speech representations with high correlation establishes an association, but does not isolate articulatory information from shared speech activity, acoustic energy, or phonetic content. Section 5.2 does not clearly specify correlation aggregation, temporal alignment, or uncertainty, and lacks controls such as speech-envelope prediction and within-active-speech evaluation. The separate gesture-clustering experiment does not establish that these same distinctions explain the speech-model correlations. Calling the layer-6 coincidence a direct explanation of downstream performance is therefore premature.

The phoneme-guidance experiment does not isolate the proposed consistency mechanism: Table 3 compares unit-only training against phoneme CTC plus consistency regularization. An auxiliary-phoneme-only condition is necessary to determine what the lookup-table consistency loss contributes. Moreover, WER and perceptual quality are evaluated only for the final system, so the claim that phoneme guidance improves generated audio is supported indirectly through UER, without a corresponding intelligibility comparison.

Important reproducibility ambiguities remain. Appendix B does not specify whether the unit-to-phoneme table is estimated exclusively from training data, and the consistency equations do not explain how the two CTC blank probabilities are handled during training. Unit-sequence deduplication, detailed vocoder configuration, and linear-probe fitting procedures also need clarification. The supplied PDF displays project, code, and data labels without usable link targets, preventing verification of the claimed releases.

Preprocessing needs reconciliation with the analyses and deployment framing. Appendix A applies per-channel, per-sentence temporal z-normalization. If this also applies to whole-trial gesture covariance estimation, its diagonal would be essentially constant, contradicting the reported power-based clustering; the applicable preprocessing must be stated separately. Sentence-wide normalization also requires future samples, so a causal TDS encoder alone does not establish a streaming pipeline.

End-to-end results demonstrate feasibility but remain limited: human WER is 62.55% for the healthy participant and 50.82% for the ALS participant. Only one participant contributes to each speech dataset, and sentence-disjoint splits do not establish robustness across recording sessions or electrode replacement. These limitations are acknowledged and do not invalidate the proof of concept, but they constrain claims about restoring functional communication. Matched comparisons with a phoneme-to-text-to-speech pipeline and synthesis from reference units would better identify the benefits and bottlenecks of direct unit generation.

Overall, the consistent decoding improvements and clinically relevant demonstration put the paper close to Findings. However, unresolved reproducibility details and insufficiently controlled evidence for two central claims—the articulatory explanation and improved synthesis through phoneme guidance—prevent a clear positive recommendation. Clarifying the implementation, adding targeted controls and ablations, and narrowing unsupported interpretations could resolve these concerns.

strengths: The paper supports a useful contribution suitable for Findings: transcript-supervised EMG-to-speech synthesis without synchronized audio targets, demonstrated on both a healthy speaker and a silently articulating participant with ALS. This is relevant to speech processing and accessible communication.

The controlled feature comparisons provide credible evidence for covariance representations. On DATA GENERAL, covariance features reduce UER from 62.71% to 56.08% and phoneme error rate from 44.40% to 32.78% relative to equally dimensional spectrogram features. Results are averaged over five seeds, and the ALS experiments show consistent improvements.

Phoneme-guided training further reduces UER on both datasets. The approach is straightforward and reuses pretrained speech components, making it a practical contribution even without a fundamentally new architecture.

Evaluation includes human transcriptions of all 460 test utterances, explicitly disjoint test sentences, and supplementary perceptual ratings. The proposed data release, including approximately nine hours from the healthy participant, could provide a valuable research resource.

The appendices provide substantial acquisition, architecture, and optimization details. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the absence of longitudinal and cross-participant validation.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Predicting EMG power from speech representations with r = 0.85 establishes association, but does not isolate articulatory information from shared speech activity, acoustic energy, or other correlates. The mel-spectrogram comparison is useful but insufficient for this distinction. Gesture clustering in a separate dataset also does not establish that articulation explains HuBERT layer 6's downstream effectiveness.

The claimed improvement in generated speech quality is evaluated only indirectly. Tables 3 and 4 show UER improvements, but human WER and MOS are reported only for the final system. Matched intelligibility evaluations of the feature and training ablations are needed to establish that their gains survive waveform synthesis. A dual-head model without the consistency loss is also needed to distinguish ordinary auxiliary phoneme supervision from the proposed regularizer.

Several details remain insufficiently specified for exact reproduction: temporal alignment and correlation aggregation for linear probing, the data partition used to estimate the unit-to-phoneme lookup table, and treatment of CTC blanks in the consistency loss. Appendix B should explicitly establish that lookup-table estimation excludes test data; the current description does not demonstrate leakage, but leaves the boundary unclear.

Streaming implications are not established by a causal encoder alone. Appendix A normalizes each channel using the complete utterance, which requires future samples, and the paper does not demonstrate streaming behavior or latency for the complete synthesis pipeline.

The clinical evidence remains a feasibility demonstration: one ALS participant, 60 test sentences, and a roughly 300-word corpus. Human WER is approximately 51% for ALS and 63% for the healthy participant. These error rates do not invalidate the research contribution, but substantially limit claims about restoring functional communication.

The main-conference case is limited by the gap between the supported empirical improvements and the broader explanatory claims. Stronger mechanistic controls, isolated training ablations, and direct comparisons of synthesized-speech intelligibility would materially strengthen that case.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to assistive speech technology: transcript-supervised EMG-to-speech synthesis without synchronized audio targets, including a demonstration using silent articulation from a participant with ALS.

Controlled comparisons support the proposed covariance representation. With the same encoder and matched feature dimensionality, covariance features reduce healthy-participant UER from 62.71% to 56.08% and PER from 44.40% to 32.78%. Results across five seeds and consistent improvements on the ALS dataset strengthen this evidence.

Phoneme-guided training further reduces UER to 51.81% on the general corpus and 46.98% on the ALS corpus. The combination of pretrained speech units, CTC, and articulatory EMG features is technically coherent.

The datasets, detailed acquisition and architecture descriptions, and stated code/data release are valuable reproducibility contributions. Human transcription of all 460 test utterances provides meaningful end-to-end evaluation beyond intermediate unit accuracy.

Overall, the supported dataset and modeling contributions warrant Findings publication. This recommendation rests on the controlled empirical results, rather than on the stronger mechanistic or clinical claims.
weaknesses: The linear-probing results support association, but do not establish the claimed mechanistic explanation for HuBERT layer 6. Shared speech activity, acoustic energy, and phonetic content could contribute to the correlations. Energy/activity controls, channel-wise results, uncertainty estimates, and clearer temporal-alignment and correlation-aggregation details would strengthen this analysis. Predictability of covariance diagonals also does not establish predictability of the full covariance representation.

The phoneme-guided experiment combines auxiliary phoneme CTC and consistency regularization. Without an auxiliary-CTC-only ablation, the benefit attributable to the proposed consistency term is unknown. Moreover, improvements are measured in UER; comparative human WER or listening evaluations are needed to substantiate improved synthesized-speech quality.

End-to-end intelligibility remains limited: human WER is 62.55% for the healthy participant and 50.82% for the ALS participant. The 3.79 MOS measures perceptual plausibility on only 35 utterances and does not establish accurate communication. These results support a proof of concept rather than restored functional speech.

Speech synthesis is evaluated on only one healthy speaker and one ALS participant, with no held-out-session or longitudinal assessment. The 12-person gesture experiment does not establish speech-decoding generalization. The paper acknowledges these limitations, but they constrain the broader claims and main-conference case.

Comparisons establish feature-level improvements more convincingly than system-level advantages. A stronger baseline under the same transcript-only supervision, particularly EMG-to-phoneme/text followed by TTS, would be informative. Appendix D.4 already reports lower WER for EMG2TEXT, but does not compare its synthesized output or latency.

Some reproducibility details remain ambiguous: Appendix B does not clearly specify which split supplies frames for the unit-to-phoneme lookup table, and handling of CTC blanks in the consistency loss needs clarification. Table 3 gives p < 10^-6 without identifying the statistical test or sampling unit. Finally, utterance-level normalization uses future samples, so the causal encoder alone does not establish streaming operation.
